title: Rivers, Landforms & Wetlands
description: How rivers shape the land — the water cycle, drainage basins, erosion and deposition, landforms from source to mouth, flooding and its management, and the value of wetlands.

notes.heading: The Water Cycle
notes.body: The water cycle (hydrological cycle) is the continuous movement of water between the sea, the air and the land. It is a closed system — the total amount of water on Earth stays the same. The main stages: (1) Evaporation — the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers, turning it into water vapour. (2) Transpiration — plants release water vapour from their leaves; together evaporation and transpiration are called evapotranspiration. (3) Condensation — water vapour cools high in the atmosphere and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. (4) Precipitation — droplets grow heavy enough to fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail. (5) Water reaching the ground then follows several paths: interception (caught by leaves), infiltration (soaking into soil), throughflow and groundwater flow (moving slowly underground), surface runoff (flowing over the land), and channel flow in rivers, which carries water back to the sea. Water can also be stored temporarily in glaciers, lakes and groundwater stores. The cycle is powered by the Sun's energy and gravity.

notes.heading: Drainage Basins
notes.body: A drainage basin is the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries — the river's 'catchment'. Its boundary is the watershed, a line of high ground separating one basin from the next: rain falling on one side flows into one river system, rain on the other side into a different one. A drainage basin works as an open system with inputs, flows, stores and outputs. The main input is precipitation. Flows and transfers include infiltration, throughflow, groundwater flow and surface runoff. Stores include soil moisture, groundwater, lakes and glaciers. Outputs are river discharge to the sea and evapotranspiration back to the atmosphere. Key features within a basin: the source (where the river begins, usually in hills or mountains), tributaries (smaller streams joining the main river), a confluence (where two rivers meet), the main channel, and the mouth (where the river ends, entering the sea or a lake). Drainage density describes how many streams a basin has per unit area — high drainage density (e.g. on clay that water cannot soak through) means rain reaches the river quickly.

notes.heading: River Processes: Erosion, Transport and Deposition
notes.body: Rivers shape the land through three linked processes. Erosion wears away the bed and banks in four ways: hydraulic action — the force of moving water itself, compressing air into cracks and breaking rock away; abrasion (corrasion) — stones carried by the river scrape and grind the bed and banks like sandpaper; attrition — stones knock against each other, breaking into smaller, rounder pieces; and solution (corrosion) — slightly acidic river water dissolves rocks such as limestone. Transportation is how the river carries its load: traction rolls large boulders along the bed; saltation bounces pebbles in short hops; suspension carries fine silt and clay within the water, making it look muddy; and solution carries dissolved minerals invisibly. Deposition happens when the river loses energy and can no longer carry its load — for example when the current slows on the inside of a bend, when the river enters a lake or the sea, or when the water level falls after a flood. The largest, heaviest material is dropped first. A river has most energy when it is fast and full, and least when shallow and slow.

notes.heading: The Upper Course: V-Shaped Valleys and Waterfalls
notes.body: A river's long profile — the slope from source to mouth — is divided into upper, middle and lower courses. The upper course lies in steep highland. The river is small, fast and full of angular boulders, and it erodes mainly downwards (vertical erosion). Downward erosion, combined with weathering and mass movement (soil slipping) on the slopes above, creates a V-shaped valley with steep sides and a narrow floor. Interlocking spurs form where the young river winds around ridges of resistant rock that jut out alternately from each side. A waterfall forms where a layer of hard, resistant rock lies over softer rock. The soft rock is eroded faster, undercutting the hard layer and creating an overhang. The overhang eventually collapses, leaving a steep plunge pool at the base. As this undercutting and collapse repeats, the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge behind it. Rapids are smaller steps of mixed hard and soft rock. Because the upper course is dominated by erosion, its features are sharp and steep.

notes.heading: Middle and Lower Courses: Meanders, Oxbow Lakes, Floodplains and Deltas
notes.body: In the middle course the gradient gentles, the river is wider and deeper, and sideways (lateral) erosion becomes as important as downward erosion. The characteristic landform is the meander — a sweeping bend. Water flows fastest around the outside of the bend, eroding the outer bank into a steep river cliff. On the inside of the bend the water is slow and shallow, so it deposits sediment, building a gently sloping slip-off slope (point bar). Over time meanders migrate sideways and downstream. An oxbow lake forms when erosion on the outer banks of a very tight bend narrows the neck of the meander until, usually during a flood, the river breaks through and takes the shorter route. Deposition then seals off the old loop, leaving a curved lake that slowly fills with sediment and dries into a meander scar. In the lower course the river is at its widest and deepest and flows across a broad, flat floodplain built up from alluvium (fertile silt) deposited during floods. Natural embankments called levees form at the channel edges, because the heaviest sediment is dropped first when floodwater spills over the banks. Where the river meets a calm sea or lake and deposits more sediment than the water can remove, the load builds up into a delta — a fan of low-lying land split by branching channels called distributaries.

notes.heading: Flooding: Causes and Management
notes.body: A flood occurs when a river's discharge exceeds the capacity of its channel, so water spills onto the floodplain. Physical causes: prolonged or intense rainfall saturates the ground so it cannot absorb more; steep slopes and impermeable rock (like granite or clay) send runoff into the river quickly; snowmelt can add a sudden surge of water. Human causes: urbanisation covers the land with tarmac and concrete, so rain rushes into drains and rivers instead of soaking in; deforestation removes the trees that intercept and use rainfall; building on floodplains puts homes directly in the flood path. Flooding can destroy homes and crops, contaminate water supplies, cause injuries and deaths, and cost millions in repairs — though floodwater also deposits fertile silt, which is why some farmers value regular floods. Management uses hard engineering — artificial structures such as dams and reservoirs (store floodwater and release it slowly), artificial levees and embankments, flood walls, and channel straightening or deepening — and soft engineering, which works with nature: planting trees upstream, restoring wetlands and meanders, creating washlands and floodplains that are allowed to flood safely, plus flood warning systems, forecasting and land-use zoning so nothing important is built in the flood zone. Soft engineering is usually cheaper and more sustainable, but hard engineering can protect towns that are already built.

notes.heading: Wetlands and Why They Matter
notes.body: A wetland is an area of land that is permanently or seasonally saturated with water — including marshes, swamps, bogs, fens, estuary mudflats and floodplain meadows. Wetlands form where water gathers: on floodplains beside slow rivers, around estuaries and deltas, and in low-lying hollows with poor drainage. Although they can look like 'wasteland', wetlands are among the most valuable ecosystems on Earth. They store floodwater like a giant sponge, soaking up heavy rain and releasing it slowly, which reduces flooding downstream. They filter water naturally — plants and mud trap sediment and absorb pollutants such as excess fertiliser, cleaning the water before it reaches rivers and the sea. They are biodiversity hotspots, providing breeding and feeding grounds for fish, frogs, dragonflies and huge numbers of migrating birds. Wetland plants also lock away carbon in waterlogged peat, helping to slow climate change. Despite this, more than a third of the world's wetlands have been drained for farming and building. Protecting and restoring wetlands is now recognised as a cheap, natural way to manage floods, improve water quality and support wildlife at the same time.

flashcards.definition: The continuous movement of water between sea, air and land through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and flow back to the sea.
flashcards.example: Ocean water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as rain on hills and returns to the sea via rivers.

flashcards.definition: The area of land drained by a river and all its tributaries; its boundary is the watershed.
flashcards.example: Every drop of rain that falls within a river's drainage basin eventually flows towards that river.

flashcards.definition: The line of high ground separating two drainage basins; rain falling either side drains into different river systems.
flashcards.example: A ridge of hills can be the watershed between two rivers flowing to opposite coasts.

flashcards.definition: River erosion where the load of stones scrapes and grinds the bed and banks, wearing them away like sandpaper.
flashcards.example: Pebbles swirling in a hollow on the river bed grind it deeper into a pothole.

flashcards.definition: River erosion where stones collide with each other, breaking into smaller, smoother and rounder pieces.
flashcards.example: Angular boulders from the upper course become rounded pebbles by the lower course.

flashcards.definition: Transport of fine silt and clay carried within the flowing water, making the river look muddy or brown.
flashcards.example: After heavy rain a river turns brown as it carries huge amounts of suspended silt.

flashcards.definition: The dropping of sediment when a river loses energy and can no longer carry its load; heaviest material is deposited first.
flashcards.example: A river slows as it enters the sea and deposits its load, building a delta.

flashcards.definition: A sudden drop in a river's course where hard rock overlying softer rock is undercut, collapses and retreats upstream, leaving a gorge.
flashcards.example: Undercutting creates an overhang of hard rock, which falls into the plunge pool below.

flashcards.definition: A sweeping bend in a river's middle or lower course, with erosion on the outer bank (river cliff) and deposition on the inner bank (slip-off slope).
flashcards.example: Water flows fastest on the outside of the bend, cutting a steep river cliff.

flashcards.definition: A curved lake formed when a river cuts through the narrow neck of a meander and the abandoned loop is sealed off by deposition.
flashcards.example: During a flood the river breaks through a meander neck, leaving the old bend stranded as an oxbow lake.

flashcards.definition: The broad, flat area of land either side of a river in its lower course, built up from fertile alluvium deposited during floods.
flashcards.example: Farmers grow crops on floodplains because the flood-deposited silt is rich in nutrients.

flashcards.definition: An area of land saturated with water, such as a marsh, swamp or bog, that stores floodwater, filters pollution and supports rich wildlife.
flashcards.example: A marsh beside a river acts like a sponge, soaking up floodwater after storms.

questions.stem: Which process in the water cycle turns liquid water from the sea into water vapour?
choices: Condensation
Precipitation
Evaporation
Infiltration
questions.explanation: Evaporation is powered by the Sun's heat, turning liquid water into vapour. Condensation is the reverse (vapour to droplets), precipitation is water falling to the ground, and infiltration is soaking into soil.

questions.stem: What is the boundary between two drainage basins called?
choices: A confluence
A watershed
A tributary
A floodplain
questions.explanation: The watershed is the line of high ground separating two basins — rain falling on either side drains into different rivers. A confluence is where two rivers meet, and a tributary is a smaller stream joining the main river.

questions.stem: Which river erosion process involves stones colliding and breaking into smaller, rounder pieces?
choices: Hydraulic action
Abrasion
Solution
Attrition
questions.explanation: Attrition is the wearing down of the load itself as stones knock together. Abrasion is stones scraping the bed and banks, hydraulic action is the force of the water, and solution is the dissolving of rock.

questions.stem: Why does a river deposit sediment on the inside of a meander bend?
choices: The water is deeper there and cannot hold sediment
The water flows slowest on the inside of the bend, so it loses energy and drops its load
The inner bank is made of sticky clay
Deposition only happens at the river's mouth
questions.explanation: The fastest current swings to the outside of a bend, leaving slow, shallow water on the inside. Slow water has less energy, so sediment is deposited, building a gentle slip-off slope.

questions.stem: Which feature is most characteristic of a river's upper course?
choices: A wide, flat floodplain
A delta
A V-shaped valley
An oxbow lake
questions.explanation: In the upper course, rapid vertical erosion combined with weathering on the slopes creates steep-sided V-shaped valleys. Floodplains, deltas and oxbow lakes form in the middle and lower courses.

questions.stem: How does a waterfall retreat upstream over time?
choices: The river dries up each summer and refills further upstream
Soft rock below the hard cap is eroded, the overhang collapses, and this undercutting repeats
The hard rock dissolves evenly across the whole ledge
Earthquakes push the waterfall backwards
questions.explanation: The softer rock layer is worn away faster, undercutting the resistant cap rock. The unsupported overhang eventually collapses into the plunge pool, and the process repeats, moving the waterfall upstream and leaving a gorge.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the formation of an oxbow lake?
choices: Deposition on the outer bank → the meander straightens → the lake drains away
Erosion narrows the meander neck → the river breaks through in a flood → deposition seals off the old loop
A dam is built → the valley floods → the river changes course
The river dries up → sediment fills the channel → a lake forms downstream
questions.explanation: Continued erosion on the outer banks narrows the meander neck. The river eventually cuts through it (often during a flood) and takes the straighter course; deposition then blocks the old loop, leaving an oxbow lake.

questions.stem: Levees are raised natural banks along a river's lower course. How do they form?
choices: People pile up earth to protect farms
When floodwater spills over the banks it slows suddenly, dropping its heaviest sediment closest to the channel
The river erodes the land on either side, leaving the banks higher
Wind blows sand onto the river banks
questions.explanation: As floodwater leaves the channel it loses energy abruptly, so the coarsest, heaviest material is deposited right at the channel edge. Repeated floods build these deposits up into natural embankments called levees.

questions.stem: Why does urbanisation increase the risk of river flooding?
choices: Cities use up all the river water for drinking
Concrete and tarmac surfaces are impermeable, so rainwater rushes into drains and rivers very quickly
Buildings block the wind that normally dries the ground
City air is too warm for rain to evaporate
questions.explanation: Impermeable surfaces stop rain soaking into the ground. Water reaches the river rapidly via drains, causing a short lag time and a high peak discharge — a flashier flood response than in a rural basin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of soft engineering flood management?
choices: Building a concrete flood wall through a town
Straightening and deepening the channel
Constructing a dam and reservoir upstream
Planting trees in the upper basin and allowing floodplains to flood safely
questions.explanation: Soft engineering works with natural processes — trees intercept rainfall and washlands store floodwater. Dams, flood walls and channel straightening are hard engineering: artificial structures that control the river directly.

choices: A steep gorge cut by a waterfall
A fan of low-lying land formed where a river deposits sediment faster than the sea or a lake can remove it
The highest point of the watershed
A curve cut off from a meander
questions.explanation: At the mouth, a river slows sharply and deposits its load. If deposition outpaces removal by tides and currents, sediment builds up into a delta, split by branching channels called distributaries.

questions.stem: Two identical rainstorms fall on two drainage basins. Basin A has steep slopes and clay soil; Basin B has gentle slopes and sandy soil. Which basin is more likely to flood, and why?
choices: Basin B — sand lets water flow too freely
Basin A — steep slopes and impermeable clay produce rapid surface runoff, so water reaches the river quickly
Both are equally likely — the same rain fell
Basin B — gentle slopes mean water cannot drain away
questions.explanation: Steep slopes speed up runoff and clay is impermeable, so little rain infiltrates — most water races into the river, causing a high, fast peak discharge. Sandy soil and gentle slopes let water soak in and arrive slowly.

questions.stem: A river transports a load of boulders, pebbles, sand and silt. If the river's velocity gradually decreases along its course, in what order will the material be deposited?
choices: Silt first, then sand, then pebbles, then boulders
All sizes are deposited at the same time
Boulders first, then pebbles, then sand, then silt
Pebbles first, then boulders, then silt, then sand
questions.explanation: Deposition follows energy: the heaviest, largest particles need the most energy to move and are dropped first as velocity falls. Fine silt can be carried in suspension even by slow water, so it travels furthest.

questions.stem: A town council must choose between building a high concrete flood wall and restoring upstream wetlands and woodlands. Which statement best compares the two options?
choices: The wall is soft engineering and cheaper; the wetland is hard engineering and expensive
The wall protects the existing town immediately but can pass the flood problem downstream; the wetland is cheaper and sustainable but protects by slowing and storing water naturally
Both are hard engineering options with identical effects
The wetland protects only the town; the wall protects the whole basin
questions.explanation: Hard engineering gives immediate, targeted protection to what already exists but is expensive and can push floodwater faster downstream. Soft engineering reduces flood risk across the basin naturally, is cheaper long-term and adds wildlife benefits, but needs land and time to work.

questions.stem: Conservationists argue that draining a marsh to create farmland is a costly mistake. Which argument supports their view most strongly?
choices: Marshes are always beautiful and should never be changed
The marsh stores floodwater, filters pollutants and supports rare wildlife — services that are expensive to replace with artificial alternatives
Farmland is worthless compared with any natural habitat
Draining marshes increases rainfall in the surrounding region
questions.explanation: Wetlands provide free ecosystem services: flood storage, natural water filtration, carbon storage and habitat for wildlife. Replacing these with reservoirs, treatment plants and flood defences costs far more than protecting the marsh.
